prompt:
Fine Print is a Victorian-detective reading-comprehension game for grades 6-12, built solo, hard deadline 26 hours out. Hackathon submission plus portfolio piece. Twelve approved design comps already exist as static HTML/CSS. The approved PRD requires an eleven-screen playable flow: study/shelf -> book opens -> vocabulary -> timed silent read -> the book closes -> word lock -> search the room -> cite the line -> reconstruct the case -> compose the conclusion from collected vocabulary -> case report.

Hard constraints from the PRD:
- The lesson is authored OFFLINE and ships as a static asset. No runtime generation, no upload, no job queue, no accounts, no user database.
- Every word the reader reads is verbatim from Project Gutenberg #269 ("The Open Window" by Saki). A verification suite must prove excerpts reconstruct exactly to source, every cited line resolves and sits inside its own excerpt, and one line numbering (1-132) holds across all screens. A Python model of this already exists and works.
- Exactly ONE live model call exists in the whole product: an "AI coach" that speaks once at the end. It receives the reader's PERFORMANCE DATA ONLY (items missed on first attempt, skill clusters, where in the excerpt the proving line sat, pace, right-answer-wrong-evidence count) and is never given the story text. If that call fails, the verdict must still render.
- Reading speed is measured and shown but never graded. Only first attempts score. Retries always allowed.

THE DOMINANT QUESTION: a model API key cannot ship in browser code, so something server-side must hold it. That single fact decides whether this is a pure static deploy or needs a server, and it gates everything else. What is the right shape for a solo dev with 26 hours who wants a live link a judge can click, when the rest of the product is genuinely static?

Also needed, with tradeoffs, ranked by what actually matters at 26 hours:
1. Frontend approach: keep the comps as hand-authored static HTML/CSS plus vanilla JS for state, or port to a framework? The comps are generated by a Python script emitting absolutely-positioned inline-styled HTML at a fixed 1440x900 - a comp technique, not a responsive app - so some rework is implied either way.
2. Where per-session state lives with no accounts (score, first attempts, cited clues, pace). It only has to survive one playthrough.
3. Model and provider choice for the coach, and how to make a single short call cheap and reliable.
4. Whether to build a pre-computed coaching fallback as demo insurance, given the live call lands at the demo's emotional peak.
5. TTS for the detective's voice: worth it at all in 26 hours, and does any option return word timings? Captions are the pre-committed fallback.
6. How the lesson file is authored and validated: extend the existing Python verification model, or collapse it into one offline generate-and-check script.
7. Project Gutenberg's terms for redistributing derived lesson content (verbatim excerpts plus authored questions) in a public demo.
8. Local toolchain gaps that could bite: Python 3.9.6 system-only, no uv, no pandoc, no API keys present yet. Node 22.22.2, npm 10.9.7, pnpm 10.33.0 available.

Bias every answer toward shipping something a judge can play in 26 hours over architectural elegance, and say plainly where you would cut.
